body.en: A sequence is just an ordered list of numbers generated by a rule; a series is what you get when you add the terms of a sequence together. AIST Math 2 tests two specific families — arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio) — and one genuinely infinite idea: a sum with infinitely many terms that still adds up to a finite number.

A sequence \( a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots \) is arithmetic if consecutive terms differ by a constant \( d \), the common difference: \( a_{n+1}=a_n+d \). Its explicit (closed-form) formula is

\[ a_n=a_1+(n-1)d. \]

An arithmetic series is the sum of an arithmetic sequence's first \( n \) terms. Pairing the first term with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on (each pair sums to \( a_1+a_n \)) gives

\[ S_n=\frac{n}{2}\big(a_1+a_n\big)=\frac{n}{2}\big(2a_1+(n-1)d\big). \]

label.en: Worked example 3.B — Sum an arithmetic series

body.en:
Find the sum of the first \( 10 \) terms of the sequence from Example 3.A (\( a_1=5,\,d=3 \)).

\[ S_{10}=\frac{10}{2}\big(2(5)+9(3)\big)=5(10+27)=5(37)=185. \]

A sequence is geometric if consecutive terms share a constant ratio \( r\neq0 \): \( a_{n+1}=r\,a_n \). Its explicit formula is

\[ a_n=a_1\,r^{\,n-1}. \]

label.en: Worked example 3.C — Find a geometric term

body.en:
A geometric sequence has \( a_1=3 \) and \( r=2 \). Find \( a_7 \).

\[ a_7=3\cdot2^{6}=3\cdot64=192. \]

For \( r\neq1 \), the sum of the first \( n \) terms of a geometric sequence is

\[ S_n=\frac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}. \]

Write out \( S_n=a_1+a_1r+a_1r^2+\cdots+a_1r^{n-1} \). Multiply both sides by \( r \): \[ rS_n=a_1r+a_1r^2+\cdots+a_1r^{n-1}+a_1r^{n}. \] Subtract the first equation from the second — every middle term cancels (this is why the trick works), leaving \[ rS_n-S_n=a_1r^{n}-a_1. \] Factor: \( S_n(r-1)=a_1(r^n-1) \), and since \( r\neq1 \) we can divide by \( r-1 \) to get \( S_n=\dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1} \). \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked example 3.D — Sum a geometric series

body.en:
If \( |r|<1 \), the infinite geometric series \( a_1+a_1r+a_1r^2+\cdots \) converges to

\[ S_\infty=\frac{a_1}{1-r}. \] If \( |r|\geq1 \) (and \( a_1\neq0 \)), the series diverges — it has no finite sum.

By Theorem 3.1, \( S_n=\dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}=\dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\big(1-r^n\big) \) (multiplying numerator and denominator by \( -1 \)). When \( |r|<1 \), repeated multiplication by a number smaller than \( 1 \) in absolute value shrinks \( r^n\to0 \) as \( n\to\infty \) (e.g. \( r=\tfrac12 \) gives \( \tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac18,\dots\to0 \)). So \( S_n\to\dfrac{a_1}{1-r}(1-0)=\dfrac{a_1}{1-r} \), which is exactly \( S_\infty \). When \( |r|\geq1 \), \( r^n \) does not shrink to \( 0 \) (it stays constant at \( |a_1| \) or grows without bound), so \( S_n \) never settles on a finite value. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked example 3.E — Sum an infinite geometric series

body.en:
Find \( 8+4+2+1+\cdots \).

Here \( a_1=8 \) and \( r=\tfrac12 \) (each term is half the last), and \( |r|=\tfrac12<1 \), so Theorem 3.2 applies: \[ S_\infty=\frac{8}{1-\tfrac12}=\frac{8}{\tfrac12}=16. \]
